title: Short Stuff: The Lost (?) Continent of Lemuria
summary: Short Stuff episode on Lemuria, the hypothetical sunken continent proposed in the mid-19th century to explain lemur distribution. Covers zoologist Philip Sclater's 1864 book The Mammals of Madagascar and his naming of Lemuria; the land-bridge theories that preceded continental drift; Ernst Haeckel's use of Lemuria as the cradle of humanity with twelve human varieties; Charles Darwin's and Charles Lyell's dismissal of sunken-continent ideas; Helena Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, her 1888 book The Secret Doctrine, and its seven root races; and the Tamil people's association with Lemuria and the Kumari Kandam legend, including Victorian British ethnologists' theories about Dravidian speakers. Hosts note there was no evidence for Lemuria and that lemurs were not actually found in India or Africa.

segments.title: Opening banter and Philip Sclater introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a ghost guest, Philip Sclater, and introduce the mid-19th century effort to explain animals and plants found on distant continents. Chuck introduces Sclater's 1864 book The Mammals of Madagascar.

segments.title: Sclater's Lemuria and the land bridge idea
segments.summary: Sclater noticed Madagascar has many lemur species while Africa and India have few or none, and proposed a sunken continent he named Lemuria to explain this. Land bridge theories were popular before continental drift was accepted in the 1920s. Hosts stress Sclater was a legitimate scientist.

segments.title: Haeckel's Lemuria as cradle of humanity
segments.summary: German biologist Ernst Haeckel adopted Lemuria in his History of Creation, claiming it was where humans evolved and that there were twelve varieties of men. Hosts say the idea had no evidence and was faulty as a basis for other hypotheses.

segments.title: Break and tangent
segments.summary: Hosts take a break; Josh jokes about Haeckel and Darwin. Brief aside.

segments.title: Darwin and Lyell reject sunken continents
segments.summary: Darwin disliked theories of sinking continents and wrote to geologist Charles Lyell, who also favored a sunken continent, mocking geologists. Hosts note Lyell was a respected scientist.

segments.title: Blavatsky, Theosophy, and The Secret Doctrine
segments.summary: Helena Blavatsky, a 19th-century Russian occultist, founded the Theosophical Society and in her 1888 book The Secret Doctrine placed Lemuria as home to the third root race, described as gigantic hermaphroditic egg-laying humans. Hosts say this helped spread Lemuria into new age and spiritualism circles.

segments.title: Lemuria today and Tamil connections
segments.summary: Hosts note modern new age sites and crystal sales tied to Lemuria. British ethnologists in colonial India linked Dravidian speakers, including Tamil people, to Lemuria. Tamil people had an existing Kumari Kandam legend of a lost civilization under the Indian Ocean and embraced the Lemuria link as proof of their antiquity.

segments.title: Closing banter and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on how attitudes toward unexplained ideas have changed, then joke about the names and close the short episode with the standard iHeartRadio credit.
